tasks.question: What has to happen to a node before a kernel upgrade?

attempts.text:
According to the documentation, a node must be drained before any kernel upgrade.

[1]

citations.title: Node maintenance
citations.quote:
## Kernel upgrades

Nodes are drained before any kernel upgrade, without exception. An in-place kernel
upgrade on a node that is still serving traffic has caused two of our three
longest outages.

Reboot the node after the packages are installed. A kernel that is installed but
not booted reports the new version to the package manager and the old version to
the running system, which makes every subsequent audit wrong.

tasks.question: How long do I have to acknowledge a page before it escalates?

attempts.text:
According to the oncall handbook, you have five minutes to acknowledge a page. If a page is still unacknowledged after ten minutes, it escalates to the secondary on-call person, and after twenty minutes, it escalates to the engineering manager.

[1]

citations.title: On-call handbook
citations.quote:
## Acknowledging a page

Acknowledge within five minutes. Acknowledging is not the same as fixing, and it
is not a commitment to fix alone — it means someone has eyes on the alert.

If a page is still unacknowledged after ten minutes it escalates to the secondary,
and after twenty to the engineering manager.

tasks.question: What happens to a webhook that cannot be delivered for a whole day?

attempts.text:
According to the document, a webhook that cannot be delivered for a whole day (twenty-four hours) is moved to a dead letter queue, and the customer is notified by email.

[1]

citations.title: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
heading_path: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
citations.quote:
## Decision

Webhook deliveries are enqueued and delivered by a separate worker pool.

The queue is durable, so a delivery survives a deploy. Retries use exponential
backoff with jitter, capped at twenty-four hours, after which the delivery is
moved to a dead letter queue and the customer is notified by email.

tasks.question: What caused the checkout latency incident INC-2451?

attempts.text: The cause of the checkout latency incident INC-2451 was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and held it for the duration of its run [3].

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## Summary

Checkout p99 latency rose from 240 ms to 9 s for 47 minutes. No requests were
lost. The cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered
by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.

tasks.question: What is the per-service connection ceiling that RB-114 step three tells me to compare against?

attempts.text:
According to RB-114 step three [2], you should compare the product of the pool size and the replica count against the per-service connection ceiling.

The per-service connection ceiling is 400, as stated in the service limits reference [1].

citations.title: RB-114: a saturated connection pool
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Read the pool utilisation for every replica, not the aggregate. An aggregate
   at 70 per cent hides one replica at 100.

2. Check whether the replica count changed in the last six hours. Each replica
   opens its own pool, so the connections a service asks for are the pool size
   multiplied by the replica count.

3. **Compare that product against the per-service connection ceiling.** The
   ceiling is a database setting and is listed in the service limits reference.
   If the product exceeds it, reduce the replica count until it does not. This is
   the step that resolves the common case, and it resolves it without a restart.

4. If the replica count did not change, look for a client holding connections
   open. Do not restart the service first: a restart clears the symptom and
   destroys the evidence, and the incident recurs on the next run of whatever was
   holding them.

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Database connections

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What happened

The nightly reconciliation job was re-enabled after the capacity review signed it
off. It ran against the dedicated pool that INC-2451's actions created, and that
pool was correctly sized. The saturation was not the job.

A deployment three hours earlier had raised the payments service replica count
from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service
connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service — so nine
replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling and the
ninth replica's connections were refused.

tasks.question: How many replicas can a payments service run on the default pool size before it hits the connection ceiling?

attempts.text:
According to the information provided in [1], the default pool size per replica is 40. The per-service connection ceiling is 400. Therefore, the maximum number of replicas that can be run on the default pool size before hitting the connection ceiling is calculated as follows:

\[ \text{Maximum replicas} = \frac{\text{Connection ceiling}}{\text{Default pool size per replica}} = \frac{400}{40} = 10 \]

So, a payments service can run **10 replicas** on the default pool size before hitting the connection ceiling.

## Steps

1. Read the pool utilisation for every replica, not the aggregate. An aggregate
   at 70 per cent hides one replica at 100.

4. If the replica count did not change, look for a client holding connections
   open. Do not restart the service first: a restart clears the symptom and
   destroys the evidence, and the incident recurs on the next run of whatever was
   holding them.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What went wrong

Replica count and connection ceiling are owned by different teams and reviewed in
different meetings. Nothing in the deployment pipeline compares the two.

The alert that fired was on authorisation failure rate. Pool utilisation was at
100 per cent for four minutes before any customer was affected, and the 80 per
cent alert that INC-2451 added had been routed to a channel nobody reads.

tasks.question: How many connections does the reconciliation job get, and do they count against the per-service ceiling?

attempts.text:
The reconciliation job has a dedicated pool of 25 connections, and these connections *are* counted against the per-service ceiling of 400 [1].

This is in contrast to the default pool size per replica, which is 40, and the ceiling being reached at ten replicas [2]. The dedicated pool for the reconciliation job is sized independently of the request pool and is not part of the default per-replica allocation [1].

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Background jobs

The reconciliation job has a dedicated pool of 25 connections, sized
independently of the request pool after INC-2451. It is not counted against the
per-replica default, but it *is* counted against the per-service ceiling of 400.

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Database connections

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What happened

The nightly reconciliation job was re-enabled after the capacity review signed it
off. It ran against the dedicated pool that INC-2451's actions created, and that
pool was correctly sized. The saturation was not the job.

A deployment three hours earlier had raised the payments service replica count
from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service
connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service — so nine
replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling and the
ninth replica's connections were refused.

citations.title: On-call handbook
citations.quote:
## Severity

Severity one means the product is unusable for a substantial share of customers,
or data is at risk. Severity two means a major feature is degraded with a
workaround. Everything else is severity three and waits for business hours.

Severity is set by impact, not by cause. A database failover that nobody noticed
is not a severity one.

citations.title: On-call handbook

## Declaring an incident

Declare an incident when customer impact is confirmed or when you need more than
one person. Declaring early costs a channel and a status page entry. Declaring
late costs the timeline, because nobody was writing anything down.

citations.title: RB-114: a saturated connection pool
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Read the pool utilisation for every replica, not the aggregate. An aggregate
   at 70 per cent hides one replica at 100.

2. Check whether the replica count changed in the last six hours. Each replica
   opens its own pool, so the connections a service asks for are the pool size
   multiplied by the replica count.

3. **Compare that product against the per-service connection ceiling.** The
   ceiling is a database setting and is listed in the service limits reference.
   If the product exceeds it, reduce the replica count until it does not. This is
   the step that resolves the common case, and it resolves it without a restart.

4. If the replica count did not change, look for a client holding connections
   open. Do not restart the service first: a restart clears the symptom and
   destroys the evidence, and the incident recurs on the next run of whatever was
   holding them.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What the on-call engineer did

The engineer followed **RB-114**, which is the procedure for a saturated pool,
and did not improvise. Step three of that runbook is what resolved this
incident. The engineer did not need to restart anything.

This postmortem deliberately does not restate RB-114's steps. A procedure copied
into a postmortem is a procedure that stops being updated, and the copy is what
somebody finds eighteen months later.

citations.title: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
heading_path: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
citations.quote:
## Consequences

Delivery is now asynchronous, so the API can no longer report whether a webhook
arrived. Customers who relied on that behaviour must poll the deliveries endpoint
instead.

A slow customer endpoint now consumes a worker from the delivery pool rather than
from the request pool, so it degrades webhook delivery for everyone but leaves the
API unaffected. That is a better failure mode, not an absent one.

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Database connections

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

tasks.question: The deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine. Why nine specifically?

attempts.text:
The deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine because the per-service connection ceiling is 400, and with a default pool size of 40 per replica, nine replicas would reach this ceiling.

[2] states: "The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any service using the default pool size."

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Database connections

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

tasks.question: Both INC-2451 and INC-3187 exhausted a connection pool. What was different about the cause?

attempts.text:
The causes of connection pool exhaustion in INC-2451 and INC-3187 were different:

- **INC-2451**: The exhaustion was caused by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and held it for the duration of its run [6].

- **INC-3187**: The exhaustion was caused by raising the payments service replica count from four to nine, which exceeded the per-service connection ceiling enforced at the database [4].

These incidents highlight different aspects of connection pool management and the importance of coordinating changes across different teams and systems [2][3].

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## Summary

Checkout p99 latency rose from 240 ms to 9 s for 47 minutes. No requests were
lost. The cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered
by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What happened

The nightly reconciliation job was re-enabled after the capacity review signed it
off. It ran against the dedicated pool that INC-2451's actions created, and that
pool was correctly sized. The saturation was not the job.

A deployment three hours earlier had raised the payments service replica count
from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service
connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service — so nine
replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling and the
ninth replica's connections were refused.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What went wrong

Replica count and connection ceiling are owned by different teams and reviewed in
different meetings. Nothing in the deployment pipeline compares the two.

The alert that fired was on authorisation failure rate. Pool utilisation was at
100 per cent for four minutes before any customer was affected, and the 80 per
cent alert that INC-2451 added had been routed to a channel nobody reads.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## Summary

Payment authorisation failed for 11 minutes on 2026-08-14. The payments service
exhausted its database connection pool for the second time in eighteen months.
The first occurrence was INC-2451.
